Baalah
bā´al-ah
n. (an older name of Kirjath-jearim, where the ark rested twenty years)
Hebrew Baalah, mistress or possessor — a Canaanite name the town carried before Israel took the land. It is identified in Scripture with Kirjath-jearim, the city of forests.

Biblical Definition

The name appears in Joshua's survey of Judah's northern boundary, with its equivalent given at once: “And the border was drawn from the top of the hill unto the fountain of the water of Nephtoah, and went out to the cities of mount Ephron; and the border was drawn to Baalah, which is Kirjathjearim” (Joshua 15:9). The line runs on past it: “And the border compassed from Baalah westward unto mount Seir, and passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, on the north side, and went down to Bethshemesh, and passed on to Timnah” (Joshua 15:10). The town matters because of what was kept there. After the Philistines returned the ark, it stood in Kirjath-jearim for twenty years, and when David finally came for it the Chronicler used the old name: “And David went up, and all Israel, to Baalah, that is, to Kirjathjearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up thence the ark of God the LORD, that dwelleth between the cherubims, whose name is called on it” (1 Chronicles 13:6). The parallel account calls the place Baale of Judah: “And David arose, and went with all the people that were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from thence the ark of God” (2 Samuel 6:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Baal as the chief male deity of the Phoenicians and Canaanites; Baalah is a town of Judah bearing the name, afterwards Kirjath-jearim.

BAALAH, n. A city on the border of Judah, the same as Kirjath-jearim, the city of forests.

BAAL, n. The chief male deity of the Phoenician and Canaanitish nations; a lord, master or possessor.

ARK, n. The chest which contained the tables of the covenant, overlaid with gold and covered with the mercy seat.

BORDER, n. The outer edge or confine of a country or district; the boundary line.

CHERUBIM, n. plu. Celestial spirits; the figures of gold that overshadowed the mercy seat.

Key Scripture

Joshua 15:9 — "And the border was drawn from the top of the hill unto the fountain of the water of Nephtoah, and went out to the cities of mount Ephron; and the border was drawn to Baalah, which is Kirjathjearim:"

Joshua 15:10 — "And the border compassed from Baalah westward unto mount Seir, and passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, on the north side, and went down to Bethshemesh, and passed on to Timnah:"

1 Chronicles 13:6 — "And David went up, and all Israel, to Baalah, that is, to Kirjathjearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up thence the ark of God the LORD, that dwelleth between the cherubims, whose name is called on it."

2 Samuel 6:2 — "And David arose, and went with all the people that were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from thence the ark of God, whose name is called by the name of the LORD of hosts that dwelleth between the cherubims."

Modern Corruption

The ark's twenty years in a private house are passed over as an administrative gap, and what that neglect says about Israel's worship goes unexamined.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the long stay at Kirjath-jearim represented. The ark was the seat of God's appointed presence between the cherubims, and for twenty years it stood in the house of Abinadab on a hill in a border town with a Canaanite name, while Israel got on with other business. Samuel's verdict on the period is that all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. The neglect was not a scheduling problem; it was a nation that had lost its centre and did not immediately notice.

The retrieval is equally instructive. David went to Baalah with thirty thousand men and a new cart, and Uzzah died reaching out to steady it, because the ark was to be carried by Levites on staves as the law required and not conveyed on Philistine equipment. David's own explanation three months later is exact: the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order. Zeal and gladness were genuine and were not enough. The same regulative instinct that governs the tabernacle's measurements governs the ark's transport, and Baalah is where Israel learned it again.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Baalah (H1173), mistress, possessor; Qiryath Yearim (H7157), city of forests; aron (H727), the ark; kerubim (H3742), cherubims.

expand to see more

Hebrew Baalah (H1173) — mistress, possessor; the older name of Kirjath-jearim.

Hebrew Qiryath Yearim (H7157) — city of forests; the name the town kept.

Hebrew Baale Yehudah — Baale of Judah, the form used in 2 Samuel 6:2.

Hebrew aron ha-elohim (H727) — the ark of God, which dwelt between the cherubims.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — due order; 1 Chronicles 15:13, we sought him not after it.

Usage

"“The border was drawn to Baalah, which is Kirjathjearim” — Judah's northern line."

"“David went up…to Baalah…to bring up thence the ark of God” — the retrieval."

"“From Baale of Judah” — the same town under a third form of the name."
